blocks.text: A 34-year-old woman has swollen, stiff small joints in both hands that are worst on waking. A blood test is positive for antibodies against cyclic citrullinated peptide, a marker so specific that its presence in a patient with inflammatory arthritis is highly suggestive of one particular diagnosis. Autoantibodies like these are among the most useful tools in diagnosing autoimmune disease.

blocks.markdown: **Autoimmune disease** is tissue damage or dysfunction caused by an adaptive immune response against self antigens. It arises when tolerance fails, through a combination of genetic susceptibility (notably particular HLA alleles), environmental triggers such as infection, and often female sex (many autoimmune diseases are more common in women). Autoimmune diseases are traditionally placed on a spectrum from **organ-specific**, where the target is one organ or cell type, to **systemic (non-organ-specific)**, where the targets are widely distributed antigens.

rows: One organ or a cell type
Tissue-restricted proteins (e.g. thyroid peroxidase, acetylcholine receptor, insulin-producing beta cell antigens)
Nucleic acids and nuclear proteins, immunoglobulin, citrullinated proteins
Type 1 diabetes, Graves disease, Hashimoto thyroiditis, myasthenia gravis, pernicious anaemia, coeliac disease
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), Sjögren syndrome, systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis (joint-predominant but systemic)
Often T cell or antibody against one organ
Often immune complexes and multi-system inflammation
blocks.caption: A spectrum rather than a strict division

blocks.title: The classification is a spectrum
blocks.text: Many diseases overlap: rheumatoid arthritis mainly affects joints but has extra-articular features; autoimmune thyroid disease may coexist with other organ-specific diseases in the same person. Use the classification as an aid, not a rule.

blocks.markdown:
**Molecular mimicry.** A microbe may carry an epitope that resembles a self antigen. An immune response mounted against the microbe can then cross-react with host tissue, causing damage after the infection has resolved. It is one proposed route by which tolerance is broken, together with others such as bystander activation and release of sequestered antigen. Well-established examples include:

- **Acute rheumatic fever** after *Streptococcus pyogenes* (group A streptococcus) pharyngitis, in which antibodies and T cells to streptococcal M protein cross-react with cardiac proteins such as myosin and valve antigens.
- **Guillain-Barré syndrome** after *Campylobacter jejuni* gastroenteritis, in which antibodies against bacterial lipo-oligosaccharide cross-react with gangliosides on peripheral nerves.

blocks.title: Rheumatic fever, step by step
blocks.prompt: A 9-year-old develops migratory joint pain, a new heart murmur and fever three weeks after untreated streptococcal pharyngitis. Explain the likely immunological mechanism.

steps.text: Identify the trigger. Group A streptococcal infection produced an immune response to the bacterial surface M protein.
Identify the cross-reaction. Some of these antibodies and T cells recognise epitopes in human cardiac myosin and valve tissue that resemble the bacterial protein (molecular mimicry).
Explain the timing. The delay of about two to four weeks reflects the time to build an adaptive response; the infection itself has resolved by the time the disease appears.

Predict consequences. Cross-reactive antibody and T cells deposit in and inflame the heart (carditis) and joints. Preventing the preceding infection with timely treatment of streptococcal pharyngitis reduces risk.

blocks.answer: Rheumatic fever is a post-infectious autoimmune disease caused by molecular mimicry between streptococcal M protein and cardiac antigens.

blocks.markdown: **Autoantibodies.** Autoantibodies are a hallmark of many autoimmune diseases. Some directly cause disease (anti-TSH receptor in Graves disease; anti-acetylcholine receptor in myasthenia gravis); others are mainly markers. Their value in diagnosis depends on **sensitivity** (fraction of patients with disease who test positive) and **specificity** (fraction without disease who test negative).

rows: SLE and other connective tissue diseases
Very sensitive for SLE, not specific; also positive in healthy people
Specific; levels may correlate with disease activity and nephritis
Less specific; also in other diseases and healthy elderly
blocks.caption: Common autoantibodies
TP, FP, TN, FN are true and false positives and negatives; PPV is positive predictive value

blocks.title: How useful is the test?
blocks.prompt: In a hypothetical study, an autoantibody test is applied to 200 patients with a disease and 300 controls. Of the patients, 150 test positive; of the controls, 6 test positive. Calculate sensitivity and specificity.

steps.text: Interpret: the test misses a quarter of patients, so a negative result does not exclude disease, but because specificity is high a positive result is strong supporting evidence.
The positive predictive value additionally depends on how common the disease is in the people tested.

items: Organ-specific disease (e.g. Graves, type 1 diabetes) and systemic disease (SLE) form a spectrum.
Molecular mimicry links infection to autoimmunity (rheumatic fever, Guillain-Barré).
Match autoantibody to disease: anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm to SLE; anti-CCP and rheumatoid factor to rheumatoid arthritis.

points: Autoimmunity spans organ-specific diseases (e.g. Graves, myasthenia gravis) and systemic diseases (e.g. SLE, rheumatoid arthritis).
Molecular mimicry between microbial and self epitopes may trigger autoimmunity, as in rheumatic fever and Guillain-Barré syndrome.
Autoantibodies support diagnosis: anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm with SLE, anti-CCP with rheumatoid arthritis, anti-TPO with Hashimoto, anti-AChR with myasthenia gravis.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a classical organ-specific autoimmune disease?

distractorRationale.b: Correct: Graves disease targets the thyroid (TSH receptor).
distractorRationale.c: Systemic sclerosis is a multisystem disease.

questions.explanation: Graves disease is mediated by antibodies against the TSH receptor in the thyroid, making it organ-specific. SLE and systemic sclerosis are non-organ-specific.

questions.stem: A woman has fatigue, malar rash, arthritis and proteinuria. Which disease class is this most consistent with?

distractorRationale.a: Several organs are affected, making a single-organ disease unlikely.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: multi-system involvement with kidneys, skin and joints suggests SLE.
distractorRationale.c: The picture is of immune activation, not deficiency.
distractorRationale.d: Type I is IgE-mediated and does not explain this pattern.

questions.explanation: Multi-organ involvement (skin, joints, kidneys) suggests a systemic autoimmune disease such as SLE, characterised by antinuclear antibodies and immune complex formation.

questions.stem: A young man develops ascending limb weakness two weeks after a Campylobacter jejuni diarrhoeal illness. Which mechanism is proposed?

options.text: Cross-reaction of anti-bacterial antibodies with peripheral nerve gangliosides
Direct invasion of nerves by Campylobacter

questions.correctOptionText: Cross-reaction of anti-bacterial antibodies with peripheral nerve gangliosides

distractorRationale.a: Correct: molecular mimicry between bacterial lipo-oligosaccharide and gangliosides.
distractorRationale.b: Complement deficiency causes infections, not this syndrome.
distractorRationale.c: The condition is post-infectious, not due to direct invasion.

questions.explanation: In Guillain-Barré syndrome after Campylobacter infection, antibodies raised against bacterial structures cross-react with peripheral nerve gangliosides, an example of molecular mimicry.

questions.stem: Which autoantibody is most specific for rheumatoid arthritis?

distractorRationale.b: Correct: anti-citrullinated peptide antibody is highly specific for RA.
distractorRationale.c: Anti-AChR is associated with myasthenia gravis.
distractorRationale.d: Anti-TPO is associated with autoimmune thyroid disease.

questions.explanation: Anti-CCP antibodies recognise citrullinated peptides and are highly specific for rheumatoid arthritis, often present before symptoms.

questions.stem: A patient with fatigue and a diffuse goitre has high anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies and a low free thyroxine. Which diagnosis fits best?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: anti-TPO with hypothyroidism suggests Hashimoto thyroiditis.
distractorRationale.b: Graves disease features hyperthyroidism and stimulating anti-TSH receptor antibodies.

questions.explanation: Anti-TPO antibodies and hypothyroidism indicate Hashimoto thyroiditis, an organ-specific autoimmune disease. Graves disease causes hyperthyroidism through stimulating antibodies.

questions.stem: True or false: acute rheumatic fever is thought to result from direct bacterial infection of the heart valves.
questions.explanation: Rheumatic fever follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis by weeks and is attributed to cross-reactive antibodies and T cells (molecular mimicry), not to bacteria in the heart.

questions.stem: In a hypothetical study of an autoantibody, 250 people without the disease are tested and 5 are positive. Calculate the specificity as a percentage.
questions.explanation: Specificity = TN/(TN+FP). With 5 false positives, TN = 245. Specificity = 245/250 = 0.98 = 98%. A high specificity means a positive result rarely occurs in people without disease.

questions.stem: A test has sensitivity 70% and specificity 95%. It is used in 1000 people, of whom 50 have the disease. Calculate the positive predictive value as a percentage.
questions.explanation: True positives = 0.70 × 50 = 35. Among 950 unaffected people false positives = 0.05 × 950 = 47.5. PPV = 35 / (35 + 47.5) = 35/82.5 = 0.424 = 42.4%. When disease is uncommon, even a specific test gives many false positives.

questions.stem: Contrast organ-specific and systemic autoimmune disease, giving two examples of each.
markingGuide: Organ-specific: single organ/cell target (e.g. Graves, type 1 diabetes, myasthenia gravis, Hashimoto)
Systemic: widely distributed antigens (e.g. SLE, systemic sclerosis, Sjögren)
questions.explanation: Organ-specific disease targets one tissue; systemic disease targets antigens present in many tissues.

questions.stem: Explain how molecular mimicry may trigger autoimmunity, using one example.
markingGuide: Response to the microbe cross-reacts with host tissue
Example: rheumatic fever (M protein with cardiac myosin) or Guillain-Barré (Campylobacter and gangliosides)
Disease appears after infection has resolved
questions.explanation: Cross-reactivity between pathogen and self lets an appropriate response become autoimmune damage.
